Having spoken thus, Ravana, the Challenger of His Foes, 
exceedingly wroth, addressed those female titans in these 
words:-
" Ye terrible demons of ferocious aspect, who subsist on 
fiesh and blood, do ye instantly crush the pride of this woman! " 
When he had said this, those monsters of fearful aspect, joining 
hands, surrounded Maithili, and Ravana commanded those 
women, formidable to look upon, who walking struck the earth 
with such force that it shook, saying :-
" Do ye take Maithili to the centre of the Ashoka grove, and 
there, encircling her mount guard over her secretly, and some-
times by menaces and at others by soft speech seek in every 
way to break her will, as one would a female elephant." 
Thus commanded by Ravana, those titan woman, taking 
hold of Maithili, dragged her to the Ashoka grove which was 
planted with trees covered with dowers of every kind and 
many fruits, able to satisfy every desire, where birds disported 
themselves in love. 
And, as a gazelle in the midst of tigresses, Sita, the daughter 
of Janaka, her limbs giving way under her despair, fell under 
the sway of those titans. 
Like a timid antelope taken in a snare, Maithili, the daughter 
of Janaka, overwhelmed with grief and fear, could find no 
relief. And threatened by those terrible monsters, the Princess 
of Mithila, unable to rest, remembering her lord and beloved 
brother-in-law, under the weight of terror and sorrow, swooned 
away.

resolved to slay Sita and for this reason Maricha, in the form 
of a gazelle, lured me away ! Having brought me a great 
distance, that titan fell a victim to my shafts and feigning my 
voice, cried out : ' 0 Lakshmana, I am slain ! ' Is all well 
with them, deprived of my presence in the forest? On account 
of Janasthana, I have rendered myself hateful to the titans, 
and many and dreadful are the portents I now see around me." 
Reflecting thus on hearing the jackals' cries, Rama hurriedly 
made his way towards the hermitage, pondering on the means 
adopted by the titan in assuming the form of a deer to lure 
him far away from his dear ones. 
Directing his steps towards Janasthana, his heart filled with 
apprehension, he observed the birds and beasts passing to his 
left, emitting fearful cries, and witnessing these dreadful 
signs Raghava beheld Lakshmana approaching, pale of mien. 
Already a prey to anxiety, Rama became even more distressed 
on seeing his brother thus cast down.

brief.summary_1line: After killing the demon Maricha, Rama hurries back to the hermitage, troubled by ominous portents and fearing Sita has been harmed.

image_candidates.scene_text: Rama runs through the forest with bow in hand while jackals howl behind him and dark birds circle ominously overhead.
Rama grasps Lakshmana’s left hand in distress, reproaching him for leaving Sita alone in the demon-haunted forest.
Pale-faced Lakshmana approaches through the woods as Rama watches anxiously, surrounded by beasts and birds crying ill omens.

deep.rich_summary: After threatening Sita, the enraged Ravana orders a band of grotesque demonesses to break her spirit. They drag the despairing princess to the Ashoka grove, a lush but prison-like garden where she will be guarded, threatened, and coaxed into yielding to him. Surrounded by terrifying watchers, Sita collapses in grief, remembering Rama and Lakshmana. Meanwhile, Rama—having slain the shape-shifting demon Maricha disguised as a deer—hurries back to the hermitage. Ominous signs fill the forest: jackals howl, beasts cry, and birds move ominously to his left. Realizing that Maricha’s dying imitation of his voice may have lured Lakshmana away, Rama fears a trap. When he finally sees Lakshmana returning alone, his anxiety deepens, and he reproaches him, convinced that terrible harm may have befallen Sita.

highlight_spans.why: Ravana’s furious command to the demonesses initiates Sita’s captivity and sets the emotional stakes for the coming search.
The transfer of Sita to the Ashoka grove establishes the central prison setting where much of her suffering and resistance will unfold.
The simile comparing Sita to a gazelle among tigresses captures her vulnerability and the emotional intensity of her isolation.
Rama’s encounter with ominous portents—howling jackals and fearful cries—signals the cosmic disturbance surrounding Sita’s abduction.

top_scenes.scene_text: Demonesses with monstrous forms drag the despairing Sita through flowering trees into the Ashoka grove while she collapses like a gazelle among tigresses.
Rama rushing through the dark forest after killing the demon-deer as jackals howl behind him and ominous birds circle overhead.
Rama grasping Lakshmana’s arm in the forest, anxiety on his face as he realizes Sita has been left alone among lurking demons.
